newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss say madcow bans could violate trade rules.
newsitem.headline: Swiss say madcow bans could violate trade rules.

text.p: Switzerland complained on Thursday that bans on its dairy and beef-related exports because of mad cow disease could violate international open trade rules.

It appealed to fellow members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to work together to ensure measures taken to fight the disease did not affect farm trade more than was necessary and legitimate, trade sources said.
After Britain, Switzerland is the country next most affected by incidences of the brain-wasting bovine illness, although its reported number of cases is tiny by comparison.
The Swiss move in the WTO's Committee on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures marked the first time any country had sought action on the issue in the trade watchdog body.

Swiss officials asked the Committee -- which oversees a 1994 agreement on health measures and trade -- to start consultations immediately on the bans in a bid to try to prevent an escalation of trade restrictions.
The sources said other countries agreed to begin discussions but made clear they would have to be open-ended and could stretch on for some considerable time.

Suspicion that the disease --known medically as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) -- could be passed on to humans through infected meat led the European Union last year to ban beef exports from Britain where most cases have been reported.
But Britain was not well-positioned to complain to the Geneva-based organisation since the EU speaks on goods trade in the WTO on behalf of all 15 member states.

From a peak of 68 in 1995 cases among its total cattle inventory of 1.75 million, Swiss officials say, the number dropped by 33 per cent last year to 45, with only 10 recorded in the second half of the year.
There had been no sign of infection from a cow to its calf or from one animal to another, and the country expects to be totally free of the disease in the near future, according to the officials.

Since 1986, about 178,000 BSE cases have been confirmed in the European Union and Switzerland, according to a European Commission information sheet. Up to the end of 1996, most of the cases -- around 172,000 -- were in Britain, followed by Switzerland with 230 and Ireland with 185, EU sources said.

In Britain on Thursday, a leading researcher of the subject said evidence was growing that people can develop the human form of BSE, known as Creuzfeldt Jakov Disease (CJD) through eating beef from cattle that had been carrying the disease.
A total of 16 probable and definite British cases of CJD have been recorded. No Swiss cases have been reported.

Trade sources said Switzerland, which exports only small quantities of beef but has a flourishing foreign trade in live cattle and bull semen and well as milk and milk products, cited some 30 countries that had BSE-linked bans.

These included its EU neighbours and major trading partners Germany, Italy and Austria as well as the United States, Canada and countries in central and eastern Europe, South East Asia, North Africa and Latin America.
Present measures in force concerned live cattle, semen, eggs, embryos, hides and skins, bones, fats, meat and bone meal, milk and milk products and some other farm produce.

Switzerland argues that these restrictions are often based on little or no scientific evidence, and fail to take into account the fact that measures it has introduced since 1990 have pushed down the already minimal BSE rate among its herds.
